source_text: ΙΒʹ. Οἱ σοφοὶ, καὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ σεμνοὶ τὴν ὑπή-νην καὶ τὸ τριβώνιον, οἱ σοφισταὶ, καὶ γραμματισταὶ, καὶ τῶν δημοσίων θηρευταὶ κρότων, οὐκ οἶδα πῶς ἂν σοφοὶ κληθείητε, τὸν πρῶτον λόγον οὐκ ἔχοντες. Οἱ περὶ τὸν πλοῦτον, ἀκούσατε τοῦ λέγοντος· Πλοῦτος ἐὰν ῥέῃ, μὴ προστίθεσθε καρδίᾳ· ἴστε θαῤῥοῦντες ἀβεβαίῳ πράγματι. Ἀποφόρτισαί τι τῆς νηὸς, ἵνα πλέῃς κουφότερος. Ἐχθροῦ τι τυχὸν ὑφαιρήσεις, εἰς ὃν τὰ σὰ περιστήσεται. Οἱ περὶ τὴν τρυ-φὴν, ὑφέλετέ τι τῆς γαστρὸς, δότε τῷ πνεύματι. Ἐγγὺς ὁ πένης· τῇ νόσῳ βοήθησον· εἰς τοῦτον ἀπέρευξαίτι τῶν περιττῶν. Τί καὶ σὺ κάμνεις ἀπεπτῶν, καὶ οὗτος πεινῶν; καὶ σὺ κραιπαλῶν, καὶ οὗτος ὑδεριῶν; καὶ σὺ κόρῳ κόρον βαρύνων, καὶ οὗτος περιτρεπόμενος νόσῳ; Μὴ παρίδῃς τὸν σὸν Λάζαρον ἐνταῦθα, μή σε ποιήσῃ τὸν ἐκεῖθεν πλού-σιον. Ὑμεῖς ἡ μεγάλη πόλις, οἱ πρῶτοι μετὰ τὴν πρώτην εὐθέως, ἢ μηδὲ τοῦτο παραχω-ροῦντες, φάνητέ μοι πρῶτοι, μὴ τὴν κακίαν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀρετήν· μὴ τὴν ἔκλυσιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν εὐνομίαν. Ὡς ἔστιν αἰσχρὸν, τῶν μὲν πόλεων κρατεῖν, τῶν δὲ ἡδονῶν ἡττᾶσθαι· ἢ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα σωφρονεῖν, περὶ δὲ τοὺς ἱππικοὺς, καὶ τὰ θέατρα, καὶ τὰ στάδια, καὶ τὰ κυνηγέσια τοσοῦτον μεμηνέναι, ὥστε ταῦτα ποιεῖσθαι βίον, καὶ πόλιν εἶναι παιζόντων τὴν πρώτην ἐν πό-λεσιν, ἣν καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις τύπον εἶναι καλοῦ παντὸς πρεπωδέστερον. Ταῦτα διαπτύοιτε, Θεοῦ πόλις εἴητε. ἐπὶ τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ Κυρίου ζωγραφηθείητε, καὶ παραστήσαισθε σὺν ἡμῖν τῷ μεγάλῳ πο-λιστῇ λαμπροὶ λαμπρῶς ὕστερον. Τοῦτο ὑμᾶς εὐαγ-γελίζομαι ἐν αὐτῷ Χριστῷ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν· ᾧ ἡ δόξα, τιμὴ, κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. Ἀμήν.
thought_title: Scolding the learned and the rich and the city to live well
orientation: Gregory closes by speaking in turn to the learned, the rich, lovers of luxury, and the great city itself to urge virtue.
pass_a_gloss: O wise ones, and philosophers, and solemn ones in beard and cloak, sophists, and schoolmasters, and hunters of public applauses, I do not know how you could be called wise, not having the first Word. O you concerned with wealth, hear the one saying: If wealth flows, do not set heart to it; know that you trust in an insecure thing. Unload something from the ship, in order that you may sail lighter. Perhaps you will take away something from an enemy, to whom your things will pass. O you concerned with luxury, take away something from the belly, give to the spirit. The poor man is near; help the sickness; belch forth into him something from the superfluous things. Why do you labor suffering from indigestion, and this one hungering? and you being drunk, and this one suffering from dropsy? and you weighing down satiety with satiety, and this one being turned about by sickness? Do not overlook your Lazarus here, lest he make you the rich man from yonder. You the great city, the first straight after the first, or not even yielding this point, appear to me first, not in vice, but in virtue; not in dissolution, but in good order. How it is shameful, to rule cities, but to be mastered by pleasures; or to be sound in other things, but concerning horse races, and theaters, and stadia, and hunts to be so mad, so as to make these things life, and for the first among cities to be a city of players, which it were more seemly to be a pattern of every fine thing to the other cities. May you spit out these things, may you be city of God. May you be painted on the hands of the Lord, and may you stand beside with us before the great citizen bright in brightness afterward. This I announce as good news to you in Christ himself our Lord; to whom be glory, honor, might unto the ages. Amen.

pass_b_english: You who are wise and learned, solemn in beard and worn cloak, you sophists and schoolmasters and hunters of public applause, I do not see how you can be called wise when you do not hold the first Word. You who cling to wealth, listen to the voice that says, "If wealth increases, do not set your heart on it" (Psalms 62:10). You know you are trusting something insecure.

Unload some cargo from your ship, so you may sail lighter. Perhaps you will snatch something from the enemy to whom all yours will pass. You who live for luxury, take something from your belly and give it to the spirit. The poor man is close at hand. Help his sickness. Belch forth into him some of your excess. Why should you labor with indigestion while he hungers? Why should you be drunk while he swells with dropsy? Why should you pile excess upon excess while he is wasted away by disease? Do not overlook your Lazarus here, or he will make you the rich man over there (Luke 16:19-31).

You, the great city, first straight after the first, or not even yielding that place, show yourselves first to me not in vice but in virtue, not in dissolution but in good order. It is shameful to rule cities yet be ruled by pleasures, to be restrained in everything else yet be so mad for horse races and theaters and stadiums and hunts that you make them your life, and the first of cities becomes a city of revelers, when it should be a fitting model of every good thing to all the rest.

May you spit out these things. May you become the city of God. May you be engraved on the hands of the Lord (Isaiah 49:16), and may you stand with us before the great founder of cities, radiant, in radiance at the last. This is the good news I bring you in Christ himself our Lord, to whom be glory, honor, and power forever. Amen.
notes: τῷ μεγάλῳ πολιστῇ read as written; sense uncertain
